activities.caption: file the properties — one model, three behaviours
activities.name: thStatesBuckets

config.prompt: The kinetic particle model explains all three states. File each property:

items.label: particles stay touching but free to slide
particles far apart, fast and random until they collide

config.why: One picture covers the ladder: vibrating solids, sliding liquids, flying gases — and melting, boiling, condensing and freezing are just transitions along it.

activities.anchor: colliding billions of times per second
activities.caption: fill the blanks — gas-law arithmetic and the kelvin rule
activities.name: thBoyleCloze

config.text: Boyle's law worked example: 0.10 m³ of air at 100 kPa compressed to 0.04 m³ gives P₂ = %%0%% kPa. And beware the scale trap: doubling a Celsius temperature does %%1%% double the pressure — only %%2%% may be doubled.
config.hint: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂; and 20 °C is 293 K while 40 °C is only 313 K.

activities.anchor: frozen pipes burst as expanding water finds no room
activities.caption: bet first — the winter lake's bottom
activities.name: thLakePredict

config.q: A lake in mid-winter, air at −10 °C, ice on top. What is the water temperature at the bottom of the lake?
choices: 0 °C — the whole lake sits at freezing
About 4 °C — water's density peak sinks below the ice
config.why: Water is the beautiful exception: it contracts as it warms from 0 to 4 °C, so 4 °C water is densest and sinks. Lakes freeze top-down, insulating the fish below.

activities.anchor: check any kettle against this and the physics passes
activities.caption: call the magnitude — your kettle's running time
activities.name: thKettleEstimate

config.prompt: A 3 kW kettle heats 1.5 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C. Roughly how long does it run?
config.why: ΔE = mc·Δθ = 1.5 × 4,186 × 80 ≈ 500 kJ; at 3,000 J/s that is about 170 s — 2.8 minutes.
config.context: Steel's c ≈ 490 is the contrast: a small iron pan screams hot while the full kettle is lukewarm on the same hob.

activities.anchor: the mantle's slow conveyor beneath the tectonic plates
activities.caption: rebuild the sea-breeze loop — convection by the coast
activities.name: thBreezeOrder

config.prompt: Put the daytime sea breeze in order:
items: Land heats faster than the sea
Air over the land warms, expands and becomes less dense
Buoyancy floats the warm air upward
Cooler sea air sinks and flows in to replace it
The loop keeps circulating — the breeze you feel on your face
config.why: Convection moves energy by moving matter: heat does not rise — the heated fluid rises. The same loop runs thunderstorm updrafts and the mantle's slow conveyor.

activities.caption: pair the property — evaporation or boiling?
activities.name: thBoilMatch

config.prompt: Related, not identical — match each property to its process:

pairs.left: happens throughout the liquid, in bubbles
loses the fastest molecules — which is why the puddle cools

config.why: Both cool what remains; only boiling demands the full latent-heat rate at one temperature — and near Everest's summit, that temperature drops to body heat.

activities.caption: true or false — steam, sweat and ice
activities.name: thSteamJudge

statements.s: Steam at 100 °C scalds worse than boiling water at 100 °C.
statements.why: Condensing on skin, steam deposits its latent heat — about 2,257 kJ/kg on top of the hot-liquid transfer.

statements.s: Evaporating sweat carries away enough energy to cool a 70 kg human by over 10 °C.
statements.why: 1.5 kg of sweat ≈ 3,600 kJ — and humidity slows evaporation, which is what makes humid heat lethal.

statements.s: Ice cools a drink only by being cold.
statements.why: Melting adds another 334 kJ/kg on top of the temperature difference — the latent half of the cooling.

statements.s: While water boils, its temperature keeps rising.
statements.why: The thermometer freezes at 100 °C — the energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds, not into jiggling.

activities.anchor: lightning charges rooftops from a distance
activities.caption: rebuild the induction sequence — charging without touching
activities.name: esInductionOrder

config.prompt: Charging by induction, step by step:
items: Bring a charged rod near a neutral sphere — electrons pile up on the near side
Earth the far side — electrons drain to or from the planet
Remove the rod — the sphere keeps a net charge opposite to the rod, never having touched it
config.why: Conservation of charge does the rest: the rod never touched the sphere, yet the sphere ends up charged — which is how lightning charges rooftops from a distance.

activities.anchor: Neutral objects are not immune; they are persuadable
activities.caption: true or false — what actually moves
activities.name: esMoveJudge

statements.s: In a rubbed rod, positive charges travel from the hair to the balloon.
statements.why: Protons are locked in nuclei; electrons do the moving — the 'positive direction' is an 18th-century convention we kept.

statements.s: A charged balloon sticks to a neutral wall because the wall's near side is induced into opposite charge.
statements.why: The near side is closer and opposite, so attraction wins — neutral objects are persuadable.

statements.s: Rubbing creates the charge that makes static electricity.
statements.why: Rubbing only separates charge; the pair's total is conserved — the balloon takes electrons, the hair loses them.

statements.s: A charged balloon carries only a vanishing fraction of its total electrons.
statements.why: About 10⁻⁸ C — some 60 billion electrons — is enough to hold it to the ceiling, yet a rounding error of the whole.

activities.anchor: which makes these forces all the more impressive
activities.caption: call the magnitude — electrons in a coulomb
activities.name: esCoulombEstimate

config.prompt: One coulomb is how many electrons' worth of charge?
config.context: A hefty static charge is a microcoulomb — 0.9 N between two of them at 10 cm, about the weight of a 90 g apple from two specks.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — field lines, plate fields and the cage
activities.name: esFieldCloze

config.text: Field lines exit %%0%% charges and enter negative ones, never crossing. Between parallel plates the uniform field has strength E = %%1%%/d, and inside a hollow conductor the interior field is exactly %%2%% — the Faraday cage.
config.hint: Think of the oscilloscope geometry, and what the free electrons rearrange until they achieve.

activities.anchor: not the route plan of anything in it
activities.caption: bet first — the electron's path between the plates
activities.name: esPathPredict

config.q: An electron enters the uniform field between two parallel plates, moving horizontally. What path does it trace through the field?
choices: It follows one of the field lines, straight across
It curves parabolically, like a thrown ball under gravity
It stops — the field blocks its motion entirely
config.why: Field lines are a map of the force, not a route plan: the electron keeps its horizontal inertia while the field bends it — a parabola, exactly like a horizontally thrown ball.

activities.anchor: watch the effects weaken as leakage improves
activities.caption: file the demos — three props, three mechanisms
activities.name: esDemosBuckets

config.prompt: Each kitchen demo runs on a different mechanism. File them:

items.label: a charged balloon holding itself to the ceiling
a charged rod bending a thin tap stream
the crackle of pulled-off cling film
lightning charging rooftops from a distance
a rubbed balloon peeling electrons off your hair

config.why: Induction bends distant objects, polar molecules explain the water stream (the near side wins by asymmetry), and friction just separates charge that already existed.

activities.anchor: every petrol station nozzle and aircraft fuelling rig has a bonding cable
activities.caption: pair each material with its electron rule
activities.name: esMatMatch

config.prompt: Match each player in the charge game to its rule:

pairs.right: charge spreads over the whole surface until repulsion balances
charge stays where it is put, which is why rubbing charges them at all
leak charge most easily — the lightning rod's trick
conductivity switched by impurities and fields — the transistor's raw material

config.why: And earthing is the universal tiebreaker: connect any conductor to the planet, and excess charge drains to neutrality — hence the bonding cable on every fuel nozzle.
